<script>
window.FE=(function(){
  const C={orange:'#d4572a',purple:'#6c5ce7',teal:'#1d9e75',gray:'#8a8a8a',pink:'#c2185b',blue:'#2e86c1',red:'#d62828'};
  function niceStep(raw){const p=Math.pow(10,Math.floor(Math.log10(raw)));const r=raw/p;return (r<1.5?1:r<3?2:r<7?5:10)*p;}
  function ticks(a,b,n){const st=niceStep((b-a)/n);const out=[];for(let v=Math.ceil(a/st-1e-9)*st;v<=b+1e-9;v+=st)out.push(Math.abs(v)<st*1e-6?0:v);return out;}
  function fmt(v){return Math.abs(v)<1e-9?'0':String(+v.toPrecision(3));}
  let clipN=0;
  function plot(id,o){
    const W=o.w||640,H=o.height||280,m={l:o.ml||58,r:20,t:22,b:o.xlabel?46:28};
    const x0=o.x[0],x1=o.x[1],y0=o.y[0],y1=o.y[1];
    const sx=v=>m.l+(v-x0)/(x1-x0)*(W-m.l-m.r), sy=v=>H-m.b-(v-y0)/(y1-y0)*(H-m.t-m.b);
    const cid='clip'+(++clipN);
    let s=`<svg viewBox="0 0 ${W} ${H}" width="100%" style="max-width:${W}px;display:block;font-size:13px" role="img" aria-label="${o.label||'plot'}">`;
    s+=`<defs><clipPath id="${cid}"><rect x="${m.l}" y="${m.t}" width="${W-m.l-m.r}" height="${H-m.t-m.b}"/></clipPath></defs>`;
    const grid='stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity="0.12"';
    (o.xtk||ticks(x0,x1,o.xt||6).map(t=>[t,fmt(t)])).forEach(([t,lab])=>{s+=`<line x1="${sx(t)}" x2="${sx(t)}" y1="${m.t}" y2="${H-m.b}" ${grid}/><text x="${sx(t)}" y="${H-m.b+16}" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">${lab}</text>`;});
    (o.ytk||ticks(y0,y1,o.yt||5).map(t=>[t,fmt(t)])).forEach(([t,lab])=>{s+=`<line x1="${m.l}" x2="${W-m.r}" y1="${sy(t)}" y2="${sy(t)}" ${grid}/><text x="${m.l-8}" y="${sy(t)+4}" text-anchor="end" fill="currentColor">${lab}</text>`;});
    if(y0<0&&y1>0)s+=`<line x1="${m.l}" x2="${W-m.r}" y1="${sy(0)}" y2="${sy(0)}" stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity="0.45"/>`;
    s+=`<line x1="${m.l}" x2="${W-m.r}" y1="${H-m.b}" y2="${H-m.b}" stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity="0.5"/>`;
    if(o.xlabel) s+=`<text x="${(m.l+W-m.r)/2}" y="${H-6}" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" opacity="0.8">${o.xlabel}</text>`;
    if(o.ylabel) s+=`<text x="${m.l}" y="${m.t-8}" text-anchor="start" fill="currentColor" opacity="0.8">${o.ylabel}</text>`;
    s+=`<g clip-path="url(#${cid})">`;
    (o.areas||[]).forEach(a=>{s+=`<polygon fill="${a.color}" fill-opacity="${a.op||0.2}" stroke="none" points="${a.pts.map(q=>sx(q[0]).toFixed(1)+','+sy(q[1]).toFixed(1)).join(' ')}"/>`;});
    (o.hlines||[]).forEach(l=>{s+=`<line x1="${m.l}" x2="${W-m.r}" y1="${sy(l.y)}" y2="${sy(l.y)}" stroke="${l.color}" stroke-width="1.6" ${l.dash?'stroke-dasharray="6 4"':''}/>`;});
    (o.lines||[]).forEach(l=>{s+=`<polyline fill="none" stroke="${l.color}" stroke-width="${l.width||2}" ${l.dash?'stroke-dasharray="6 4"':''} stroke-linejoin="round" points="${l.pts.filter(q=>isFinite(q[1])).map(q=>sx(q[0]).toFixed(1)+','+sy(q[1]).toFixed(1)).join(' ')}"/>`;});
    (o.dots||[]).forEach(d=>{s+=`<circle cx="${sx(d.x)}" cy="${sy(d.y)}" r="${d.r||5}" fill="${d.color}"/>`;});
    (o.texts||[]).forEach(t=>{s+=`<text x="${sx(t.x)+(t.dx||0)}" y="${sy(t.y)+(t.dy||0)}" text-anchor="${t.anchor||'middle'}" fill="${t.color||'currentColor'}">${t.text}</text>`;});
    s+='</g></svg>';
    if(o.legend) s+='<div class="fe-legend">'+o.legend.map(l=>`<span><i style="border-color:${l.color};${l.dash?'border-top-style:dashed;':''}"></i>${l.label}</span>`).join('')+'</div>';
    document.getElementById(id).innerHTML=s;
  }
  function val(id){return +document.getElementById(id).value;}
  function show(id){const e=document.getElementById(id),st=String(e.step||'1');const d=st.includes('.')?st.split('.')[1].length:0;const o=document.getElementById(id+'-v');if(o)o.textContent=(+e.value).toFixed(d);}
  function bind(ids,fn){ids.forEach(id=>{document.getElementById(id).addEventListener('input',()=>{show(id);fn();});show(id);});fn();}
  function span(vals,pad){let a=Math.min(...vals),b=Math.max(...vals);if(b-a<1e-12){a-=1;b+=1;}const p=(b-a)*(pad||0.12);return [a-p,b+p];}
  function TB(head,rows){let s='<'+'table class="fe-table">';
    if(head)s+='<tr>'+head.map(h=>'<th>'+h+'</th>').join('')+'</tr>';
    rows.forEach(r=>{s+='<tr>'+r.map((c,i)=>{if(i===0)return '<th>'+c+'</th>';let cls='';
      if(typeof c==='object'&&c){cls=c.cls||'';c=c.v;}
      return '<td'+(cls?' class="'+cls+'"':'')+'>'+c+'</td>';}).join('')+'</tr>';});
    return s+'</table>';}
  function band(K,F,bw){const n=F.length,A=K.map(r=>r.slice()),b=F.slice();
    for(let i=0;i<n;i++)for(let r=i+1;r<=Math.min(n-1,i+bw);r++){const m=A[r][i]/A[i][i];if(!m)continue;
      for(let c=i;c<=Math.min(n-1,i+bw);c++)A[r][c]-=m*A[i][c];b[r]-=m*b[i];}
    const d=new Array(n).fill(0);for(let i=n-1;i>=0;i--){let s=b[i];for(let c=i+1;c<=Math.min(n-1,i+bw);c++)s-=A[i][c]*d[c];d[i]=s/A[i][i];}return d;}
  function gauss(n){const x=[],w=[];for(let i=1;i<=n;i++){let z=Math.cos(Math.PI*(i-0.25)/(n+0.5)),pp=1;
      for(let it=0;it<100;it++){let p1=1,p2=0;for(let j=1;j<=n;j++){const p3=p2;p2=p1;p1=((2*j-1)*z*p2-(j-1)*p3)/j;}
        pp=n*(z*p1-p2)/(z*z-1);const z1=z;z=z1-p1/pp;if(Math.abs(z-z1)<1e-15)break;}
      x.push(z);w.push(2/((1-z*z)*pp*pp));}return {x,w};}
  const SUP={'-':'⁻','0':'⁰','1':'¹','2':'²','3':'³','4':'⁴','5':'⁵','6':'⁶','7':'⁷','8':'⁸','9':'⁹'};
  function sup(n){return String(n).split('').map(c=>SUP[c]||c).join('');}
  function fmtE(v){if(!isFinite(v))return '—';if(Math.abs(v)<1e-300)return '0';const e=Math.floor(Math.log10(Math.abs(v)));
    if(e>=-3&&e<=3)return String(+v.toPrecision(4));return (v/Math.pow(10,e)).toFixed(3)+'×10'+sup(e);}
  return {C,plot,val,bind,show,span,TB,band,gauss,sup,fmtE};
})();
</script>

# Part 0: What is this section *for*?

::: {.goal}
**Goal of Section 4.1.** Chapters 1–3 built a machine: choose shape functions, form $\boldsymbol{K}$ and $\boldsymbol{F}$ element by element, solve $\boldsymbol{K}\boldsymbol{d}=\boldsymbol{F}$. Nothing in those chapters says the numbers that come out are *close* to the true answer, or that refining the mesh helps. Section 4.1 is the **theory of trust**. In Hughes's words, it will "establish the convergence of the finite element methodology considered so far and show, in addition, that in a sense it is an optimal technique," and then end with "a caution regarding the application of these ideas to certain classes of problems."
:::

There are three promises and one warning:

| | Claim | Where in the text | Plain meaning |
|--|--------|----------|--------------------|
| 1 | **Best approximation** | Theorem, parts (a) and (b); Corollary; part (c) | On *one fixed mesh*, among every function that mesh can possibly build, the FE answer is the closest to the exact solution, measured in energy. |
| 2 | **Convergence rates** | (4.1.6), fundamental error estimate, standard estimate, Aubin–Nitsche | As the elements shrink ($h\to0$), the error goes to zero like $h^{p}$, and the power $p$ is computable from the element type and the problem. |
| 3 | **Survives quadrature** | "Effect of Numerical Quadrature" | If the Gauss rule is exact through a stated polynomial degree, the rates in promise 2 are unchanged. |
| ⚠ | **The catch** | "Discussion" | "Best" can still be terrible if *nothing* your mesh can build is close to the truth. That is **locking**, and it is why Sections 4.2 onward exist. |

Notice that promises 1 and 2 are different *kinds* of statement:

- **Promise 1** is about a single mesh at a finite $h$. It says nothing about how big the error is, only that no other choice on this mesh does better.
- **Promise 2** is about what happens as $h\to0$. It says how big the error is, but only as a trend, and only if the true solution is smooth enough.

The argument chains like this, and the rest of the page walks down it:

```{.ascii}
  Part 2: exact weak form  &  FE weak form   (same equation, different sets of functions)
                      │
                      ▼   subtract them
  Part 4: error is a-orthogonal to the mesh space      (Theorem a)
                      │
                      ▼   Pythagoras
          FE answer = closest point in the mesh space  (Theorem b)
                      │
                      ▼   "closest" ≤ "connect-the-dots", and connect-the-dots is ≈ h^α
  Part 5: ‖error‖ ≤ c̄ h^α ‖u‖                          (fundamental estimate)
                      │
                      ▼   but only if every integral is done exactly enough
  Part 6: Gauss rule exact through degree k̄ + k − 2m   (quadrature rule)
                      │
                      ▼   and only if some function in the mesh space IS close to u
  Part 7: constrained problems break this              (locking)
```

## Cheat sheet: every symbol in Section 4.1

Come back to this table whenever a symbol is unfamiliar. The "first used" column points to the step where the symbol is defined with a picture.

| Symbol | What it is | In mechanics words | First used |
|------|----------------|--------------|----|
| $\boldsymbol{u}$ | the **exact** solution | true temperature / displacement field | 10 |
| $\boldsymbol{u}^h$ | the **FE** solution (lowercase, one specific function) | what your code returns | 8 |
| $\boldsymbol{U}^h$ | **any** function the mesh can build (capital = "candidate") | a trial answer, right or wrong | 8 |
| $\boldsymbol{w},\ \boldsymbol{w}^h$ | **weighting (test) functions**, exact space / mesh space | virtual displacements | 7 |
| $\boldsymbol{e}=\boldsymbol{u}^h-\boldsymbol{u}$ | the error function | error in the temperature/displacement field | 15 |
| $\mathcal{S},\ \mathcal{V}$ | sets of exact **trial** / **test** functions | admissible displacements / virtual displacements | 8 |
| $\mathcal{S}^h,\ \mathcal{V}^h$ | the **mesh** versions of $\mathcal{S},\mathcal{V}$ | everything the mesh can represent | 8 |
| $a(\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{u})$ | energy inner product (bilinear form) | $\int \varepsilon(w):C:\varepsilon(u)\,d\Omega$ | 5 |
| $(\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{f})$ | $\int_\Omega \boldsymbol{w}\cdot\boldsymbol{f}\,d\Omega$ | work of the body load | 7 |
| $(\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{h})_\Gamma$ | $\int_\Gamma \boldsymbol{w}\cdot\boldsymbol{h}\,d\Gamma$ | work of boundary tractions / flux | 7 |
| $a(\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{w})^{1/2}$ | **energy norm** | square root of twice the strain energy | 5 |
| $\lVert\boldsymbol{w}\rVert_m$ | **Sobolev norm** (values and derivatives up to order $m$) | an "overall size" ruler | 5 |
| $m$ | highest derivative order in $a(\cdot,\cdot)$ | 1 for heat and solids, 2 for beams | 5 |
| $k$ | polynomial degree the shape functions reproduce **completely** | 1 = linear, 2 = quadratic | 21, 29 |
| $\bar k$ | highest degree of **any** monomial present | 2 for a bilinear quad | 29 |
| $h$ | **mesh parameter** (size of the largest element) | element size | 21 |
| $r$ | how many derivatives of $u$ are square-integrable | smoothness of the true solution | 21 |
| $c_1,c_2,c,\bar c$ | constants that don't depend on $h$ or $u$ | — | 6, 21, 22 |
| $\alpha,\ \beta$ | exponents in the error bounds | rates of convergence | 21, 23 |

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## Heads-up: three different letter h's
Hughes uses $h$ for three unrelated things in this one section:

1. $\boldsymbol{h}$ in $(\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{h})_\Gamma$ (**bold**): prescribed **boundary flux / traction**.
2. $h$ in $\lVert\cdot\rVert\le c\,h^{\alpha}$ (plain): the **mesh size**.
3. The superscript in $\boldsymbol{u}^h,\ \mathcal{S}^h$: just a tag meaning "built from the mesh."

Context always tells you which. In our worked example there is no boundary flux, so $\boldsymbol{h}$ only means mesh size.
:::



# Part 1: The toolkit, from scratch

::: {.goal}
**Goal of this part.** Hughes's theorem is, underneath, a statement from plane geometry: *the closest point on a line to a given point is where you drop a perpendicular.* To read it you need four ideas, each of which is just "the plane picture, applied to functions": **inner product**, **perpendicular**, **norm (length)**, and **projection**. We build them for ordinary arrows first, then promote them to functions.
:::

## 1. Arrows: inner product, length, perpendicular

Take two arrows (vectors) in the plane, $\boldsymbol{x}=(x_1,x_2)$ and $\boldsymbol{y}=(y_1,y_2)$. Their **inner product** (dot product) is

$$
\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{y}=x_1y_1+x_2y_2 .
$$

- Length: $|\boldsymbol{x}|=\sqrt{\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}}=\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}$ (Pythagoras).
- Perpendicular: $\boldsymbol{x}\perp\boldsymbol{y}$ exactly when $\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{y}=0$.

Three properties of this product matter, because Hughes demands exactly these from his $a(\cdot,\cdot)$:

| Property | Statement | Hughes's word |
|-----|-----------------|---------|
| **bilinear** | $(\alpha\boldsymbol{x}+\beta\boldsymbol{y})\cdot\boldsymbol{z}=\alpha\,\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{z}+\beta\,\boldsymbol{y}\cdot\boldsymbol{z}$, and the same in the second slot | "bilinear" (assumption ii) |
| **symmetric** | $\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{y}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}$ | "symmetric" (assumption ii) |
| **positive** | $\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}>0$ unless $\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}$ | follows from "equivalent norms" (assumption iii) |

*Where:* $\alpha,\beta$ are any numbers; "linear in a slot" means you can split sums and pull out constants, which is all "bilinear" means ("bi" because there are two slots).

The one algebraic move you'll see repeatedly is **FOIL**, which is bilinearity plus symmetry:

$$
(\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{y})\cdot(\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{y})=\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}+2\,\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{y}+\boldsymbol{y}\cdot\boldsymbol{y}.
$$

The middle term is $2\,\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{y}$ (not two different terms) *because of symmetry*: $\boldsymbol{x}\cdot\boldsymbol{y}+\boldsymbol{y}\cdot\boldsymbol{x}$. Hold that thought: it is where Hughes's proof of part (b) uses symmetry.

## 2. A different ruler: the matrix inner product

You can build other inner products from a **symmetric positive-definite (SPD) matrix** $\boldsymbol{A}$:

$$
\langle\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}\rangle_{A}=\boldsymbol{x}^{T}\boldsymbol{A}\,\boldsymbol{y}.
$$

*Where:* $\boldsymbol{x}^T$ is the row version of $\boldsymbol{x}$; "symmetric" means $\boldsymbol{A}^T=\boldsymbol{A}$; "positive-definite" means $\boldsymbol{x}^T\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}>0$ for every nonzero $\boldsymbol{x}$.

Example: $\boldsymbol{A}=\begin{bmatrix}2&0.8\\0.8&1\end{bmatrix}$. Then

$$
\boldsymbol{x}^T\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}=2x_1^2+1.6\,x_1x_2+x_2^2
=2\,(x_1+0.4\,x_2)^2+0.68\,x_2^2 ,
$$

(completing the square), which is positive unless both squares vanish, i.e. unless $\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}$. So $\boldsymbol{A}$ is SPD, and $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_A$ obeys all three properties above.

With this ruler, "perpendicular" means $\boldsymbol{x}^T\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}=0$, which **does not look perpendicular on paper**. Two arrows at 60° can be "$A$-perpendicular." That is not a trick: it is exactly the situation in FE. The stiffness matrix $\boldsymbol{K}$ plays the role of $\boldsymbol{A}$ (you'll see $a(U^h,V^h)=\boldsymbol{c}^T\boldsymbol{K}\boldsymbol{d}$ in step 12), so Hughes's "orthogonal" is $\boldsymbol{K}$-orthogonal.

## 3. Projection: the closest point on a line

**Setup.** A line through the origin in direction $\boldsymbol{b}$: $\mathcal{L}=\{t\,\boldsymbol{b}\}$ (every multiple of $\boldsymbol{b}$). A point $\boldsymbol{u}$ off the line. **Question:** which point $t\boldsymbol{b}$ on the line is closest to $\boldsymbol{u}$?

Score every candidate by the squared distance and FOIL it:

$$
E(t)=|\boldsymbol{u}-t\boldsymbol{b}|^2=\underbrace{\boldsymbol{u}\cdot\boldsymbol{u}}_{\text{constant}}\;-\;2t\,(\boldsymbol{u}\cdot\boldsymbol{b})\;+\;t^2\,(\boldsymbol{b}\cdot\boldsymbol{b}).
$$

*Where:* $t$ is the one unknown (how far along the line); $\boldsymbol{u}\cdot\boldsymbol{u}$ is a fixed number.

This is a parabola in $t$: a **bowl** (opening up because $\boldsymbol{b}\cdot\boldsymbol{b}>0$). The bottom is where the slope is zero:

$$
\frac{dE}{dt}=-2\,\boldsymbol{u}\cdot\boldsymbol{b}+2t\,\boldsymbol{b}\cdot\boldsymbol{b}=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
t^{*}=\frac{\boldsymbol{u}\cdot\boldsymbol{b}}{\boldsymbol{b}\cdot\boldsymbol{b}} .
$$

Now look at the leftover arrow, $\boldsymbol{e}^{*}=\boldsymbol{u}-t^{*}\boldsymbol{b}$:

$$
\boldsymbol{e}^{*}\cdot\boldsymbol{b}=\boldsymbol{u}\cdot\boldsymbol{b}-t^{*}\,\boldsymbol{b}\cdot\boldsymbol{b}=0 .
$$

**The error at the bottom of the bowl is perpendicular to the line.** "Minimize the distance" and "make the error perpendicular" are the same statement. And Pythagoras then holds for any other candidate $t\boldsymbol{b}$:

$$
|\boldsymbol{u}-t\boldsymbol{b}|^2=|\boldsymbol{u}-t^{*}\boldsymbol{b}|^2+|(t-t^{*})\,\boldsymbol{b}|^2\;\ge\;|\boldsymbol{u}-t^{*}\boldsymbol{b}|^2 .
$$

(The two legs are the error $\boldsymbol{e}^*$ and the slide along the line, which are perpendicular.) *Every* step of Hughes's proof is this paragraph with new names. Try it:

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## What to do
Pick the **Euclidean** ruler first: drag the candidate $t$ and watch the squared distance. Press **Snap** to jump to the closest point and note that the error arrow meets the line at 90°. Then switch to the **Energy ruler** ($\boldsymbol{A}$ from step 2). The closest point *moves*, and the error no longer looks perpendicular, but the readout shows the $\boldsymbol{A}$-inner product with the line is zero. Check Pythagoras in the last readout line.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="fe-widget" id="pj">
<div class="fe-btns"><button id="pj-eu" class="on">Euclidean ruler (A = identity)</button><button id="pj-en">Energy ruler (A = [[2, 0.8], [0.8, 1]])</button><button id="pj-snap">Snap to closest point</button></div>
<div class="fe-ctrl wide">
<label for="pj-th">direction of the line (°)</label><input type="range" id="pj-th" min="0" max="170" step="1" value="20"><output id="pj-th-v"></output>
<label for="pj-t">candidate position t</label><input type="range" id="pj-t" min="-1" max="3" step="0.01" value="0.4"><output id="pj-t-v"></output>
</div>
<div id="pj-plot"></div>
<div id="pj-out" class="fe-out"></div>
</div>
<script>
(function(){
  const $=id=>document.getElementById(id);
  const U=[2.0,1.5];            // the "exact solution" point u
  let energy=false;
  const A=()=>energy?[[2,0.8],[0.8,1]]:[[1,0],[0,1]];
  const ip=(x,y)=>{const a=A();return x[0]*(a[0][0]*y[0]+a[0][1]*y[1])+x[1]*(a[1][0]*y[0]+a[1][1]*y[1]);};
  const sub=(x,y)=>[x[0]-y[0],x[1]-y[1]];
  function geom(){const th=FE.val('pj-th')*Math.PI/180,b=[Math.cos(th),Math.sin(th)],tstar=ip(U,b)/ip(b,b);return {b,tstar};}
  function render(){
    const {b,tstar}=geom(),t=FE.val('pj-t'),C=[t*b[0],t*b[1]],B=[tstar*b[0],tstar*b[1]];
    const d2=ip(sub(U,C),sub(U,C)),dstar=ip(sub(U,B),sub(U,B)),slide=ip(sub(C,B),sub(C,B)),orth=ip(sub(U,B),b);
    const L=4,ln=[[-L*b[0],-L*b[1]],[L*b[0],L*b[1]]];
    const W=520,H=360,m=36,x0=-1.5,x1=4.5,y0=-1.5,y1=3.5;
    const sx=v=>m+(v-x0)/(x1-x0)*(W-2*m), sy=v=>H-m-(v-y0)/(y1-y0)*(H-2*m);
    let s=`<svg viewBox="0 0 ${W} ${H}" width="100%" style="max-width:${W}px;display:block;font-size:13px" role="img" aria-label="projection onto a line">`;
    s+=`<line x1="${sx(x0)}" x2="${sx(x1)}" y1="${sy(0)}" y2="${sy(0)}" stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity=".2"/><line x1="${sx(0)}" x2="${sx(0)}" y1="${sy(y0)}" y2="${sy(y1)}" stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity=".2"/>`;
    s+=`<line x1="${sx(ln[0][0])}" y1="${sy(ln[0][1])}" x2="${sx(ln[1][0])}" y2="${sy(ln[1][1])}" stroke="${FE.C.purple}" stroke-width="3" stroke-opacity=".7"/>`;
    s+=`<text x="${sx(3.2*b[0])+8}" y="${sy(3.2*b[1])-8}" fill="${FE.C.purple}">mesh space 𝒮ʰ (a line)</text>`;
    s+=`<line x1="${sx(U[0])}" y1="${sy(U[1])}" x2="${sx(B[0])}" y2="${sy(B[1])}" stroke="${FE.C.orange}" stroke-width="2.4"/>`;
    s+=`<line x1="${sx(U[0])}" y1="${sy(U[1])}" x2="${sx(C[0])}" y2="${sy(C[1])}" stroke="${FE.C.gray}" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/>`;
    s+=`<line x1="${sx(B[0])}" y1="${sy(B[1])}" x2="${sx(C[0])}" y2="${sy(C[1])}" stroke="${FE.C.teal}" stroke-width="2.4"/>`;
    s+=`<circle cx="${sx(U[0])}" cy="${sy(U[1])}" r="7" fill="${FE.C.red}"/><text x="${sx(U[0])+10}" y="${sy(U[1])-6}" fill="currentColor">u (exact)</text>`;
    s+=`<circle cx="${sx(B[0])}" cy="${sy(B[1])}" r="6" fill="${FE.C.orange}"/><text x="${sx(B[0])+10}" y="${sy(B[1])+18}" fill="${FE.C.orange}">uʰ (closest)</text>`;
    s+=`<circle cx="${sx(C[0])}" cy="${sy(C[1])}" r="5.5" fill="${FE.C.gray}"/><text x="${sx(C[0])-8}" y="${sy(C[1])+18}" text-anchor="end" fill="currentColor">Uʰ (your candidate)</text>`;
    s+='</svg>';
    s+='<div class="fe-legend"><span><i style="border-color:'+FE.C.orange+'"></i>error of the best point, e = uʰ − u</span><span><i style="border-color:'+FE.C.gray+';border-top-style:dashed"></i>error of your candidate, Uʰ − u</span><span><i style="border-color:'+FE.C.teal+'"></i>the slide along the line, Uʰ − uʰ</span></div>';
    $('pj-plot').innerHTML=s;
    const f=v=>v.toFixed(3),nm=energy?'energy ruler':'Euclidean ruler';
    let o='<b>'+nm+'.</b> Squared distance of your candidate, |Uʰ − u|² = <b>'+f(d2)+'</b>; of the closest point, |uʰ − u|² = <b>'+f(dstar)+'</b>.<br>';
    o+='Inner product of the best error with the line direction: ⟨uʰ − u, b⟩ = <b>'+(Math.abs(orth)<1e-9?'0':f(orth))+'</b>'+(energy?' &nbsp;(zero in the energy ruler, even though the arrow doesn\'t look perpendicular)':'')+'<br>';
    o+='Pythagoras check: |uʰ − u|² + |Uʰ − uʰ|² = '+f(dstar)+' + '+f(slide)+' = <b>'+f(dstar+slide)+'</b> &nbsp;vs&nbsp; |Uʰ − u|² = <b>'+f(d2)+'</b>';
    $('pj-out').innerHTML=o;
  }
  FE.bind(['pj-th','pj-t'],render);
  $('pj-eu').addEventListener('click',()=>{energy=false;$('pj-eu').classList.add('on');$('pj-en').classList.remove('on');render();});
  $('pj-en').addEventListener('click',()=>{energy=true;$('pj-en').classList.add('on');$('pj-eu').classList.remove('on');render();});
  $('pj-snap').addEventListener('click',()=>{const t=geom().tstar;const e=$('pj-t');e.value=Math.max(-1,Math.min(3,t));FE.show('pj-t');render();});
})();
</script>
```

**Things to notice:**

1. In the Euclidean ruler the orange error arrow is perpendicular to the purple line. Change the line's direction and the closest point slides, but the right angle stays.
2. In the energy ruler the closest point is a *different* point, and the error arrow is visibly slanted. "Closest" depends on the ruler. FE's ruler is the energy ruler.
3. The Pythagoras line always balances. That one identity is the entire content of Theorem part (b).

## 4. Functions are arrows too

A function $w(x)$ on $0\le x\le1$ is "a list of numbers, one for each $x$": its value at every point. You can **add** two functions and **scale** a function, exactly as with arrows. So collections of functions can be treated as spaces of arrows with *infinitely* many components.

Now look at what a mesh can build. Take the two-element bar from step 11 below: one unknown $d$, and every candidate is $U^h(x)=d\,N_1(x)$, where $N_1$ is the hat function. All multiples of $N_1$: **a line through the origin in function space**. With $n$ unknown nodal values, $U^h=\sum_B d_B N_B$ is an $n$-dimensional flat sheet (a "subspace") sitting inside the infinite-dimensional space of all admissible functions.

| Plane picture | Function-space picture |
|---|---|
| the point $\boldsymbol{u}$ | the exact solution $u(x)$ |
| the line $\mathcal{L}$ | the mesh space $\mathcal{S}^h$ (everything the mesh can build) |
| the closest point on $\mathcal{L}$ | the FE solution $u^h$ |
| the error arrow $\boldsymbol{u}-t^*\boldsymbol{b}$ | the error function $e=u^h-u$ |
| the ruler $\boldsymbol{x}^T\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{y}$ | the energy product $a(\cdot,\cdot)$ |

That table *is* Hughes's sentence: "$u^h$ is the projection of $u$ onto $\mathcal{S}^h$ with respect to $a(\cdot,\cdot)$."

## 5. Inner products and norms of functions

To measure lengths you need an inner product *of functions*. Replace the sum $\sum x_iy_i$ by an integral. The two that appear in 4.1 (in 1D):

$$
(w,v)=\int_0^1 w\,v\,dx
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
a(w,v)=\int_0^1 \kappa\,w_{,x}\,v_{,x}\,dx .
$$

*Where:* $w,v$ are two functions; $\kappa$ is the conductivity (the weight in the energy ruler); a comma means a derivative, so $w_{,x}=dw/dx$.

For elasticity the energy product is $a(\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{u})=\int_\Omega \varepsilon(\boldsymbol{w}):\boldsymbol{C}:\varepsilon(\boldsymbol{u})\,d\Omega$, with $\varepsilon$ the strain (the symmetric part of the gradient) and $\boldsymbol{C}$ the elastic constants. Hughes writes this with indices: $w_{(i,j)}\,c_{ijkl}\,u_{(k,l)}$.

**Check the three properties for the heat form** (this is what "assumption (ii)" asks of you):

- *Bilinear:* the integral is linear and so is differentiation, so $a(\alpha w+\beta v,z)=\alpha a(w,z)+\beta a(v,z)$.
- *Symmetric:* $\kappa w_{,x}v_{,x}=\kappa v_{,x}w_{,x}$, so $a(w,v)=a(v,w)$.
- *Positive:* $a(w,w)=\int\kappa\,w_{,x}^2\,dx\ge0$, and it is $0$ only if $w_{,x}=0$ everywhere, i.e. $w$ is constant. If $w(0)=0$ is enforced, a constant must be $0$. So $a(w,w)=0\Rightarrow w=0$.

(Note that the load terms $(w,f)$ and $(w,h)_\Gamma$ are *not* inner products of two unknowns: each is **linear in $w$** and contains a given function. They are the "right-hand side.")

**Norm = length from an inner product.** $\lVert w\rVert=(w,w)^{1/2}$ for the plain product, and $a(w,w)^{1/2}$ for the energy product, which Hughes calls the **(strain) energy norm**. In mechanics terms, $a(e,e)$ is *twice the strain energy stored in the error field*.

**The Sobolev norms** (4.1.4) measure values *and* derivatives. In 1D, the $m$th one is the square root of the integral of $w^2$ plus every squared derivative up to order $m$:

| Norm | Formula | Measures |
|---|-----------|------|
| $\lVert w\rVert_0$ | $\Big(\displaystyle\int w^2\,dx\Big)^{1/2}$ | values only |
| $\lVert w\rVert_1$ | $\Big(\displaystyle\int \big(w^2+w_{,x}^2\big)\,dx\Big)^{1/2}$ | values and slopes |
| $\lVert w\rVert_2$ | $\Big(\displaystyle\int \big(w^2+w_{,x}^2+w_{,xx}^2\big)\,dx\Big)^{1/2}$ | values, slopes, curvatures |

Hughes writes it for 3D vector fields, which is why (4.1.4) looks heavy:

$$
\lVert\boldsymbol{w}\rVert_m=\Big[\int_\Omega\big(w_iw_i+w_{i,j}w_{i,j}+\cdots+\underbrace{w_{i,jk\ldots l}}_{m\text{ indices}}\underbrace{w_{i,jk\ldots l}}_{m\text{ indices}}\big)\,d\Omega\Big]^{1/2}.
$$

Decode it with three facts:

- $\boldsymbol{w}$ is a **vector field**: a rule that attaches a vector $(w_1,w_2,w_3)$ to every point of the body (a displacement field is one).
- A **comma means differentiate**: $w_{i,j}=\partial w_i/\partial x_j$. Collect all of these for $i,j=1,2,3$ and you get a $3\times3$ array of derivatives: the **gradient (Jacobian matrix) of the field**.
- A **repeated index is summed**: $w_iw_i=w_1^2+w_2^2+w_3^2$ and $w_{i,j}w_{i,j}$ = the sum of the squares of all nine entries. So it is the same "square it and add it up" as in the 1D table, just with more components.

**What the letter $m$ in $\lVert\cdot\rVert_m$ and in assumption (iii) means:** the highest derivative that appears inside $a(\cdot,\cdot)$. Heat and elasticity energy has first derivatives, so $m=1$. A Bernoulli–Euler beam's energy has curvature $w_{,xx}$, so $m=2$.

**Mechanics translation of two rulers you'll use constantly:**

- $\lVert e\rVert_0$: size of the error in **displacement** (or temperature).
- $\lVert e\rVert_1$ (and the energy norm, which is equivalent to it): size of the error in **strain, stress, heat flux**, since those are first derivatives.

## 6. Norm equivalence (assumption iii): why two rulers agree

Hughes's (4.1.3) says there are constants $c_1,c_2>0$, independent of $w$, with

$$
c_1\,\lVert w\rVert_m\;\le\;a(w,w)^{1/2}\;\le\;c_2\,\lVert w\rVert_m\qquad\text{for every } w\in\mathcal{V}.
$$

*Where:* $\mathcal{V}$ is the set of test functions (zero at the fixed boundary, step 8); the energy ruler sits between two copies of the Sobolev ruler.

Read it as: **"small in one ruler" and "small in the other" are the same thing, up to the fixed factors $c_1,c_2$.** The upper bound ($c_2$) says energy can't be large if the function is small; the lower bound ($c_1$) says energy can't be tiny if the function is big. The lower bound is the interesting one, and it is where the supports (boundary conditions) enter.

For the bar with both ends fixed, take the test function $w=\sin(n\pi x)$ (a pinned wiggle with $n$ half-waves). Then (integrals done in the widget below)

$$
a(w,w)=\int_0^1 w_{,x}^2\,dx=\frac{n^2\pi^2}{2},\qquad
\lVert w\rVert_1^2=\int_0^1\!\big(w^2+w_{,x}^2\big)dx=\frac{1+n^2\pi^2}{2},
$$

so the ratio is

$$
\frac{a(w,w)^{1/2}}{\lVert w\rVert_1}=\frac{n\pi}{\sqrt{1+n^2\pi^2}} .
$$

For $n=1$ that is $0.953$ and for large $n$ it tends to $1$: it is trapped between $c_1\approx0.95$ and $c_2=1$.

Now remove the support. Allow a **constant offset** $c$: $w=c+\sin(n\pi x)$. This $w$ no longer vanishes at the ends, so it is *not* in $\mathcal{V}$, but it is what an unsupported model would allow. Slide $c$ up in the widget and the ratio collapses toward $0$: a big function with almost no energy. No $c_1>0$ exists.

```{=html}
<div class="fe-widget" id="nm">
<div class="fe-ctrl wide">
<label for="nm-n">half-waves n</label><input type="range" id="nm-n" min="1" max="12" step="1" value="1"><output id="nm-n-v"></output>
<label for="nm-c">offset c (0 = both ends fixed)</label><input type="range" id="nm-c" min="0" max="3" step="0.05" value="0"><output id="nm-c-v"></output>
</div>
<div class="fe-row">
  <div><p class="fe-cap"><b>The function</b> w(x) = c + sin(nπx)</p><div id="nm-w"></div></div>
  <div><p class="fe-cap"><b>The ratio</b> energy norm ÷ ‖w‖₁ as the offset c grows</p><div id="nm-r"></div></div>
</div>
<div id="nm-out" class="fe-out"></div>
</div>
<script>
(function(){
  const $=id=>document.getElementById(id),G=FE.gauss(24);
  function integ(f){let s=0;for(let g=0;g<24;g++)s+=G.w[g]*0.5*f(0.5+0.5*G.x[g]);return s;}
  const C1=Math.sqrt(Math.PI**2/(1+Math.PI**2));
  function ratio(n,c){const w=x=>c+Math.sin(n*Math.PI*x),wp=x=>n*Math.PI*Math.cos(n*Math.PI*x);
    const a=integ(x=>wp(x)**2),n0=integ(x=>w(x)**2);return {a:Math.sqrt(a),n1:Math.sqrt(a+n0),R:Math.sqrt(a)/Math.sqrt(a+n0)};}
  function run(){
    const n=FE.val('nm-n'),c=FE.val('nm-c'),r=ratio(n,c);
    const pts=[];for(let i=0;i<=200;i++){const x=i/200;pts.push([x,c+Math.sin(n*Math.PI*x)]);}
    FE.plot('nm-w',{w:420,x:[0,1],y:[-1.2,4.2],height:260,label:'the function',xlabel:'x',lines:[{pts,color:FE.C.purple,width:2.4}],
      dots:[{x:0,y:c,color:FE.C.orange,r:5},{x:1,y:c,color:FE.C.orange,r:5}]});
    const curve=[];for(let i=0;i<=60;i++){const cc=3*i/60;curve.push([cc,ratio(n,cc).R]);}
    FE.plot('nm-r',{w:420,x:[0,3],y:[0,1.1],height:260,label:'ratio versus offset',xlabel:'offset c',ml:50,
      areas:[{pts:[[0,C1],[3,C1],[3,1],[0,1]],color:FE.C.teal,op:0.22}],
      hlines:[{y:1,color:FE.C.teal,dash:true},{y:C1,color:FE.C.teal,dash:true}],lines:[{pts:curve,color:FE.C.purple,width:2.4}],
      dots:[{x:c,y:r.R,color:FE.C.orange,r:6}],legend:[{label:'green band: c₁ ≈ 0.953 to c₂ = 1 (valid only for c = 0)',color:FE.C.teal}]});
    const f=v=>v.toFixed(4),inb=r.R>=C1-1e-9;
    $('nm-out').innerHTML='Energy norm a(w,w)<sup>1/2</sup> = <b>'+f(r.a)+'</b> &nbsp; ‖w‖₁ = <b>'+f(r.n1)+'</b> &nbsp; ratio = <b>'+f(r.R)+'</b>'
      +(c===0?'<div class="fe-status fe-ok">Both ends fixed: the ratio stays inside the band for every n. That is the equivalence of norms.</div>'
        :inb?'<div class="fe-status fe-warn">The ratio has started to drop. Keep raising c.</div>'
        :'<div class="fe-status fe-bad">Ratio below the band: a function with large size but small energy. Without supports, norm equivalence fails (and the stiffness matrix would be singular: a rigid-body mode costs no energy).</div>');
  }
  FE.bind(['nm-n','nm-c'],run);
})();
</script>
```

::: {.eng}
**Engineer's reading.** A constant temperature (or a rigid-body displacement) stores no energy. If the model has no supports, such a mode is allowed, so a big function can have zero energy and (iii) fails. That's the theory version of "a model with no supports has a singular $\boldsymbol{K}$," and the reason your solver refuses to run it.
:::



# Part 2: The two problems and the rules of the game

::: {.goal}
**Goal of this part.** Hughes writes the exact problem and the FE problem as *the same equation* with different function sets. Everything in the theorem follows from that sameness, so we must see precisely (1) what the equation says, (2) which functions are allowed in each version, and (3) what the three numbered assumptions (i)–(iii) buy us and what breaks when they fail.
:::

## 7. The exact problem (4.1.1)

Hughes's abstract weak form: **find $\boldsymbol{u}\in\mathcal{S}$ such that for all $\boldsymbol{w}\in\mathcal{V}$,**

$$
\boxed{a(\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{u})=(\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{f})+(\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{h})_\Gamma}\tag{4.1.1}
$$

*Where:* $a(\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{u})$ is the energy product of step 5 (left side: how the weighting function $\boldsymbol{w}$ "feels" the solution's gradients); $(\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{f})=\int_\Omega\boldsymbol{w}\cdot\boldsymbol{f}\,d\Omega$ is the work of the body load $\boldsymbol{f}$ (heat source, gravity) through $\boldsymbol{w}$; $(\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{h})_\Gamma=\int_\Gamma\boldsymbol{w}\cdot\boldsymbol{h}\,d\Gamma$ is the same for the boundary flux/traction $\boldsymbol{h}$ on the part $\Gamma$ of the boundary where it is prescribed. "For all $\boldsymbol{w}$" means the equation must hold for every test function in the set $\mathcal{V}$, not just one.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Where this comes from (the Chapter 1 recap, for the 1D bar)
Start from the strong form $-(\kappa u_{,x})_{,x}=f$ on $0<x<1$. Multiply by a test function $w$ and integrate:

$$
\int_0^1 w\,\big(-(\kappa u_{,x})_{,x}\big)\,dx=\int_0^1 w f\,dx .
$$

Integrate the left side by parts ($\int p\,q'\,dx=[pq]-\int p'q\,dx$ with $p=w$, $q=-\kappa u_{,x}$):

$$
\int_0^1 w_{,x}\,\kappa u_{,x}\,dx-\Big[w\,\kappa u_{,x}\Big]_0^1=\int_0^1 w f\,dx .
$$

The bracket is the boundary term. Where $u$ is prescribed (essential BC) we force $w=0$, so that end contributes nothing. Where the flux is prescribed (natural BC), the bracket turns into $(w,h)_\Gamma$ (a given number times $w$ at that end). What remains is exactly (4.1.1) with $a(w,u)=\int w_{,x}\kappa u_{,x}\,dx$. The derivative on $u$ has been *shared* with $w$: that is why one derivative per slot is all $a$ needs, and why linear shape functions work.
:::

## 8. The four sets of functions

This is the vocabulary that trips people up. Hughes uses four function sets:

| Set | What is in it | Condition on the boundary | Used for |
|--|---------|---------|-------|
| $\mathcal{S}$ | exact **trial** functions $\boldsymbol{u}$ | satisfy the given essential BC, $\boldsymbol{u}=\boldsymbol{g}$ on $\Gamma_g$; finite energy | where the exact $\boldsymbol{u}$ lives |
| $\mathcal{V}$ | exact **weighting (test)** functions $\boldsymbol{w}$ | **homogeneous** essential BC, $\boldsymbol{w}=\boldsymbol{0}$ on $\Gamma_g$; finite energy | what we multiply the equation by |
| $\mathcal{S}^h$ | **mesh-built** trial functions $\boldsymbol{u}^h,\ \boldsymbol{U}^h$ | built from shape functions; satisfy $\boldsymbol{g}$ at the fixed nodes | where the FE answer lives |
| $\mathcal{V}^h$ | **mesh-built** test functions $\boldsymbol{w}^h$ | built from shape functions; zero at the fixed nodes | what FE multiplies by |

"Finite energy" means $a(w,w)<\infty$. Our tiny bar (step 11) will make this concrete: $\mathcal{V}$ is *all* sensible functions with $w(0)=w(1)=0$, and $\mathcal{V}^h$ is just *tents*: multiples of the single hat function.

**The FE problem (4.1.2)** is the same sentence, hatted: *find $\boldsymbol{u}^h\in\mathcal{S}^h$ such that for all $\boldsymbol{w}^h\in\mathcal{V}^h$,*

$$
\boxed{a(\boldsymbol{w}^h,\boldsymbol{u}^h)=(\boldsymbol{w}^h,\boldsymbol{f})+(\boldsymbol{w}^h,\boldsymbol{h})_\Gamma}\tag{4.1.2}
$$

Same $a$, same load terms, same $\boldsymbol{f}$ and $\boldsymbol{h}$. Only the function sets shrank. (This is the Galerkin method: use the *same* shape functions for $\boldsymbol{w}^h$ as for $\boldsymbol{u}^h$.)

**Why is $\mathcal{S}$ different from $\mathcal{V}$?** If the fixed temperature is $g\neq0$, then adding two members of $\mathcal{S}$ gives a function equal to $2g$ on the boundary, which is *not* in $\mathcal{S}$. So $\mathcal{S}$ isn't closed under addition, but **the difference of two members of $\mathcal{S}$ is zero on $\Gamma_g$, hence is a member of $\mathcal{V}$.** That one fact is the hinge of the whole proof: it is why the error $e=u^h-u$ and the gap $U^h-u^h$ are legal test functions.

**Reading the lowercase/uppercase code:**

- $\boldsymbol{u}$: *the* exact solution.
- $\boldsymbol{u}^h$: *the* FE solution, the one function in $\mathcal{S}^h$ that solves (4.1.2).
- $\boldsymbol{U}^h$: *any* member of $\mathcal{S}^h$, a candidate. Theorem (b) compares $\boldsymbol{u}^h$ against all of them.

## 9. The three assumptions, and what each is for

Hughes lists three assumptions that hold "throughout." Don't skim these: every failure mode of FE in practice is a broken assumption.

| | Assumption | What it means in practice | Where the proof uses it | What violates it |
|--|------|-------|-------|-------|
| **(i)** | $\mathcal{S}^h\subset\mathcal{S}$ and $\mathcal{V}^h\subset\mathcal{V}$ | **Conforming** elements: everything the mesh can build is a legitimate exact candidate (continuous, right BCs, finite energy). | Step 15 (can use $w^h$ in the *exact* equation); step 16 ($U^h-u^h$ lies in $\mathcal{V}^h$); part (c). | Non-conforming elements (gaps or jumps across element edges), elements that fail the patch test, mismatched meshes joined without constraints. |
| **(ii)** | $a(\cdot,\cdot)$, $(\cdot,\cdot)$, $(\cdot,\cdot)_\Gamma$ are **symmetric and bilinear** | A symmetric energy: self-adjoint problem. | Bilinearity: the subtraction in (a). Symmetry: collapsing the cross terms in (b) and in the corollary. | Convection-dominated transport, follower/nonconservative loads, anything with a non-symmetric tangent. |
| **(iii)** | $c_1\lVert w\rVert_m\le a(w,w)^{1/2}\le c_2\lVert w\rVert_m$ on $\mathcal{V}$ | The problem is **well-posed**: enough supports, material positive-definite. | Gives *strict* best approximation (step 16), and the ruler switch in the fundamental estimate (step 22). | Rigid-body modes (no supports), materials that lose positive-definiteness, constraints that make $c_1$ tiny. |

::: {.aha}
**Read this table as a debugging guide.** If a mesh behaves oddly, ask: which assumption did I just break? A **non-conforming** element breaks (i). A **convection-dominated** problem breaks (ii). A model with **missing supports** breaks (iii). The theory is telling you precisely what must be true for the guarantees to apply.
:::



# Part 3: One tiny example, done completely

::: {.goal}
**Goal of this part.** Before the general proof, do the whole story on a problem small enough to hold in your head: *one* unknown. We will score every possible answer the mesh can build, see that the score is a **bowl**, and find that **the bottom of the bowl is exactly $\boldsymbol{K}\boldsymbol{d}=\boldsymbol{F}$.** That coincidence is Hughes's theorem in miniature.
:::

## 10. Our tiny problem

A bar from $x=0$ to $x=1$, both ends held at $u=0$, uniform heat source $f=1$, conductivity $\kappa=1$:

$$
-u_{,xx}=1,\qquad u(0)=u(1)=0 .
$$

Integrating twice and fitting both ends gives the exact solution

$$
\boxed{u(x)=\frac{x(1-x)}{2}},\qquad u_{,x}=\tfrac12-x .
$$

*Check:* $u_{,xx}=-1$ ✓, $u(0)=0$ ✓, $u(1)=0$ ✓.

Because the ends are fixed at $0$, the boundary condition is *homogeneous*, so $\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{V}$ here (and $\mathcal{S}^h=\mathcal{V}^h$), and there's no flux boundary, so $(\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{h})_\Gamma=0$. Our weak form is simply

$$
a(w,u)=(w,f),\qquad a(w,u)=\int_0^1 w_{,x}u_{,x}\,dx,\quad (w,f)=\int_0^1 w\,dx .
$$

## 11. Every answer our mesh can build

Use **two linear elements**:

```{.ascii}
 u = 0                                u = 0
   ●─────────────────●─────────────────●
  x=0   element 1   x=½   element 2   x=1
                     d
             (the one unknown)
```

Both ends are fixed, so the only unknown is the temperature $d$ at the middle node. Every function the mesh can build is

$$
U^h(x)=d\,N_1(x),
$$

where $N_1$ is the **hat function** for the middle node: $N_1(0)=0$, $N_1(\tfrac12)=1$, $N_1(1)=0$, linear in between. So $\mathcal{S}^h=\mathcal{V}^h=\{\text{all tents } d\,N_1\}$: **one knob, $d$.** Taller $d$, taller tent.

> **Which $d$ is best?** "Best" means closest to the exact $u$ in the energy ruler.

## 12. Score every tent: the error bowl

The energy-ruler squared error of the tent with knob $d$ is

$$
E(d)=a\big(U^h-u,\;U^h-u\big).
$$

FOIL it (bilinear + symmetric, step 1):

$$
E(d)=\underbrace{a(U^h,U^h)}_{\text{piece 1}}-2\,\underbrace{a(U^h,u)}_{\text{piece 2}}+\underbrace{a(u,u)}_{\text{piece 3}} .
$$

Let's do it for **any number of unknowns** at once, since it costs nothing extra. Write $U^h=\sum_{B}d_B\,N_B$, with $N_B$ the shape functions of the free nodes and $d_B$ the unknown nodal values. (Our case is a single term, $U^h=d\,N_1$.)

**Piece 1.** Pull the sums and constants out of both slots (bilinearity):

$$
a(U^h,U^h)=a\Big(\sum_A d_AN_A,\ \sum_B d_BN_B\Big)=\sum_A\sum_B d_A\,\underbrace{a(N_A,N_B)}_{K_{AB}}\,d_B=\boldsymbol{d}^T\boldsymbol{K}\boldsymbol{d}.
$$

*Where:* $K_{AB}=a(N_A,N_B)$ is exactly the stiffness matrix entry from Chapter 2 (the energy product of two shape functions). So piece 1 is "the energy of the candidate," $\boldsymbol{d}^T\boldsymbol{K}\boldsymbol{d}$.

**Piece 2.** Pull out the sum:

$$
a(U^h,u)=\sum_A d_A\,a(N_A,u).
$$

Here is the problem: this contains the *unknown exact solution* $u$. The weak form hands us a way out. Each $N_A$ is zero at the fixed ends, so $N_A\in\mathcal{V}$, which means we are allowed to plug $w=N_A$ into the **exact** equation (4.1.1):

$$
a(N_A,u)=(N_A,f)+(N_A,h)_\Gamma=:F_A .
$$

And $F_A$ is precisely the load vector entry. So

$$
a(U^h,u)=\sum_A d_AF_A=\boldsymbol{d}^T\boldsymbol{F}.
$$

::: {.aha}
**This is the trick that makes FE possible.** We were scoring tents against the true solution, which we don't know, and the equation of the problem *evaluates the unknown for us*. The error bowl can be written down without ever knowing $u$.
:::

**Piece 3.** $a(u,u)$ is one fixed number. It shifts the bowl up or down but does not move its bottom.

Collecting the three pieces:

$$
\boxed{E(\boldsymbol{d})=\boldsymbol{d}^T\boldsymbol{K}\boldsymbol{d}-2\,\boldsymbol{d}^T\boldsymbol{F}+a(u,u)}
$$

**Find the bottom.** For two unknowns, written out in full (using $K_{12}=K_{21}$):

$$
E=K_{11}d_1^2+2K_{12}d_1d_2+K_{22}d_2^2-2F_1d_1-2F_2d_2+a(u,u).
$$

Set each partial derivative to zero:

$$
\frac{\partial E}{\partial d_1}=2K_{11}d_1+2K_{12}d_2-2F_1=0,\qquad
\frac{\partial E}{\partial d_2}=2K_{12}d_1+2K_{22}d_2-2F_2=0 .
$$

Divide by 2 and stack the two lines:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}K_{11}&K_{12}\\K_{12}&K_{22}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}d_1\\d_2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}F_1\\F_2\end{bmatrix}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\boldsymbol{K}\boldsymbol{d}=\boldsymbol{F}.
$$

The same works for any number of unknowns: $\nabla_{\boldsymbol{d}}E=2(\boldsymbol{K}\boldsymbol{d}-\boldsymbol{F})$.

::: {.aha}
**Solving $\boldsymbol{K}\boldsymbol{d}=\boldsymbol{F}$ is the same thing as finding the tent with the smallest energy error.** FE never knew $u$, yet it found the bottom of a bowl defined by $u$.
:::

**Is it a bowl and not a saddle or a hill?** The curvature of $E$ is governed by $\boldsymbol{d}^T\boldsymbol{K}\boldsymbol{d}=a(U^h,U^h)$, which is positive for every nonzero $\boldsymbol{d}$ by assumption (iii) (step 5: $a(w,w)=0\Rightarrow w=0$). A matrix with $\boldsymbol{d}^T\boldsymbol{K}\boldsymbol{d}>0$ for all $\boldsymbol{d}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$ is **symmetric positive-definite**, so $\boldsymbol{K}$ is invertible and the bowl has one unique bottom. That is why the Cholesky-type solvers apply, and why a model with no supports (singular $\boldsymbol{K}$) has a *flat-bottomed trough* instead of a bowl: infinitely many "best" answers.

## 13. The numbers for our tiny bar

**Piece 1 (the stiffness).** $N_1$ climbs from 0 to 1 over a length $\tfrac12$, so its slope is $+2$ on the left half and $-2$ on the right half:

$$
K=a(N_1,N_1)=\int_0^{1/2}(2)^2dx+\int_{1/2}^{1}(-2)^2dx=4\cdot\tfrac12+4\cdot\tfrac12=4 .
$$

(Assembly check: each element's stiffness is $\kappa/h_e=1/(1/2)=2$ on the diagonal, and the middle node gets $2+2=4$. ✓)

**Piece 2 (the load).** $F=(N_1,f)=\int_0^1N_1\cdot1\,dx$ = the area of the tent = $\tfrac12\cdot1\cdot1=\tfrac12$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Don't trust the trick? Check it by brute force
Compute $a(N_1,u)$ directly with the true $u_{,x}=\tfrac12-x$:

$$
a(N_1,u)=\int_0^{1/2}2\big(\tfrac12-x\big)dx+\int_{1/2}^{1}(-2)\big(\tfrac12-x\big)dx .
$$

First integral: $2\big[\tfrac x2-\tfrac{x^2}2\big]_0^{1/2}=2\big(\tfrac14-\tfrac18\big)=\tfrac14$.
Second: $-2\big[\tfrac x2-\tfrac{x^2}2\big]_{1/2}^{1}=-2\big(0-\tfrac18\big)=\tfrac14$.
Total $\tfrac12$ ✓. It equals $F$, with no mention of $u$ in the definition of $F$.
:::

**Piece 3 (the true energy).** $a(u,u)=\int_0^1\big(\tfrac12-x\big)^2dx=\tfrac1{12}$.

The bowl is

$$
E(d)=4d^2-d+\tfrac1{12}.
$$

The bottom: $dE/dd=8d-1=0\Rightarrow d=\tfrac18$, i.e. $Kd=F$ with $4d=\tfrac12$. The smallest possible energy error is

$$
E\big(\tfrac18\big)=4\cdot\tfrac1{64}-\tfrac18+\tfrac1{12}=\tfrac1{16}-\tfrac18+\tfrac1{12}=\frac{3-6+4}{48}=\frac1{48}.
$$

(The exact $u(\tfrac12)=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12/2=\tfrac18$ too: for a *uniform* 1D bar FE is exact at the nodes. That is a coincidence of 1D with constant $\kappa$. The bonus button in the widget breaks it, and the answer is *still* the bottom of the bowl: "best" means best in energy, not best at the nodes.)

## 14. Try it yourself

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## What to do
Drag the tent height $d$ and watch the error score. Try to find a tent with less error than the FE answer (you can't). Press **Jump** and check the bowl's slope is exactly zero. Then press the **tapered** button and see that FE misses the true middle temperature yet is still at the bottom of the bowl.
:::

  function setup(M){const K=integ(x=>4*M.kap(x),0,0.5)+integ(x=>4*M.kap(x),0.5,1);
    const Auu=integ(x=>M.kap(x)*M.up(x)**2,0,0.5)+integ(x=>M.kap(x)*M.up(x)**2,0.5,1);return {K,F:0.5,Auu,dFE:0.5/K};}
  let mode='uni',P=setup(MODES.uni),d=0.2;

      +'<b>Slope of the bowl:</b> dE/dd = 2(Kd − F) = '+(Math.abs(slope)<1e-12?'0':slope.toFixed(4));
    s+=atFE?'<div class="fe-status fe-ok"><b>You\'re at the bottom.</b> The slope of the bowl is zero, so Kd = F. This tent is the FE solution uʰ, and no other tent has a smaller error score.</div>'

But the exact temperature at the middle is u(½) = '+f4(M.u(0.5))+'. FE gets the nodal temperature <b>wrong</b>, and it\'s still at the bottom of the bowl. **Things to notice:**

1. Drag $d$ and the purple dot slides along a bowl. The orange dot at the bottom is the FE answer.
2. Press **Jump**. The slope of the bowl becomes exactly zero, and $Kd=F$.
3. At the FE answer, look at the slope plot. On each element, the shaded area above the line equals the area below it: the FE slope is the **average** of the true slope over the element. That is what "best fit of the slopes" looks like.
4. The **tapered** button: FE misses the true temperature at the middle node, yet it is still at the bottom of the bowl. "Best" refers to the energy ruler, not to matching values.



# Part 4: The theorem, and why it's true

::: {.goal}
**Goal of this part.** Show, for *any* mesh and *any* number of unknowns, what Part 3 showed for one: **FE's answer is the closest point in the mesh space to the exact solution, in the energy ruler.** Then collect the free bonuses: Pythagoras for energies, "FE is too stiff," and the potential-energy statement in part (c).
:::

## 15. The box, and part (a): the error is perpendicular to the mesh space

Hughes's boxed theorem: let $\boldsymbol{e}=\boldsymbol{u}^h-\boldsymbol{u}$ be the error. Then

$$
\boxed{\begin{aligned}
&\text{(a)}\quad a(\boldsymbol{w}^h,\boldsymbol{e})=0 &&\text{for all }\boldsymbol{w}^h\in\mathcal{V}^h,\\
&\text{(b)}\quad a(\boldsymbol{e},\boldsymbol{e})\le a(\boldsymbol{U}^h-\boldsymbol{u},\,\boldsymbol{U}^h-\boldsymbol{u}) &&\text{for all }\boldsymbol{U}^h\in\mathcal{S}^h.
\end{aligned}}
$$

*Where:* (a) says $\boldsymbol{e}$ is $a$-orthogonal to every test function the mesh can build; (b) says the squared energy error of the FE answer is no bigger than that of any other candidate $\boldsymbol{U}^h$.

**Proof of (a).** Two equations, same right-hand side:

- The exact equation (4.1.1) holds for every $\boldsymbol{w}\in\mathcal{V}$. By assumption (i), $\mathcal{V}^h\subset\mathcal{V}$, so it holds in particular for every $\boldsymbol{w}^h\in\mathcal{V}^h$: $\;a(\boldsymbol{w}^h,\boldsymbol{u})=(\boldsymbol{w}^h,\boldsymbol{f})+(\boldsymbol{w}^h,\boldsymbol{h})_\Gamma$.
- The FE equation (4.1.2): $\;a(\boldsymbol{w}^h,\boldsymbol{u}^h)=(\boldsymbol{w}^h,\boldsymbol{f})+(\boldsymbol{w}^h,\boldsymbol{h})_\Gamma$.

Subtract the first from the second. The right-hand sides cancel, and bilinearity combines the left-hand sides:

$$
0=a(\boldsymbol{w}^h,\boldsymbol{u}^h)-a(\boldsymbol{w}^h,\boldsymbol{u})=a(\boldsymbol{w}^h,\boldsymbol{u}^h-\boldsymbol{u})=a(\boldsymbol{w}^h,\boldsymbol{e}).\qquad\blacksquare
$$

Notice what happened: **the whole thing rests on the two problems being the *same equation* tested on nested function sets.** (i) is what lets the same $\boldsymbol{w}^h$ be used in both.

**In our tiny bar:** $a(N_1,e)=a(N_1,u^h)-a(N_1,u)=Kd-F=4\cdot\tfrac18-\tfrac12=0$ ✓. Orthogonality is just $\boldsymbol{K}\boldsymbol{d}=\boldsymbol{F}$ in disguise: the residual of the matrix equation *is* the inner product of the error with each shape function.

**Mechanics translation.** For heat, $a(w^h,e)=\int w^h_{,x}\,\kappa\,e_{,x}\,dx=0$: the flux error $\kappa e_{,x}$ does no "work" against the gradient of any mesh function. Equivalently, the FE solution satisfies conservation/equilibrium **in the weighted-average sense of the mesh's own test functions** ($\boldsymbol{K}\boldsymbol{d}=\boldsymbol{F}$ holds exactly), not point by point.

## 16. Proof of (b): Pythagoras, line by line

**Idea:** compare the FE answer $\boldsymbol{u}^h$ with an arbitrary competitor $\boldsymbol{U}^h$. The step from $\boldsymbol{u}^h$ to $\boldsymbol{U}^h$ is a move *within the mesh space*, and by (a) the error is perpendicular to such moves.

1. **Define the gap** $\boldsymbol{w}^h:=\boldsymbol{U}^h-\boldsymbol{u}^h$. Then $\boldsymbol{U}^h=\boldsymbol{u}^h+\boldsymbol{w}^h$, which is Hughes's "any $\boldsymbol{U}^h\in\mathcal{S}^h$ can be written as $\boldsymbol{u}^h+\boldsymbol{w}^h$."

   **Is $\boldsymbol{w}^h$ a legal test function?** Both $\boldsymbol{U}^h$ and $\boldsymbol{u}^h$ lie in $\mathcal{S}^h$, so both equal $\boldsymbol{g}$ on the fixed boundary. Their difference is zero there, and it is built from shape functions, so $\boldsymbol{w}^h\in\mathcal{V}^h$. (This is the "difference of trial functions is a test function" fact from step 8.)

2. **Rewrite the competitor's error:**

$$
\boldsymbol{U}^h-\boldsymbol{u}=(\boldsymbol{u}^h-\boldsymbol{u})+(\boldsymbol{U}^h-\boldsymbol{u}^h)=\boldsymbol{e}+\boldsymbol{w}^h .
$$

3. **FOIL its energy** (bilinearity, then symmetry to merge the two cross terms):

$$
a(\boldsymbol{e}+\boldsymbol{w}^h,\,\boldsymbol{e}+\boldsymbol{w}^h)=a(\boldsymbol{e},\boldsymbol{e})+\underbrace{a(\boldsymbol{e},\boldsymbol{w}^h)+a(\boldsymbol{w}^h,\boldsymbol{e})}_{=\,2a(\boldsymbol{w}^h,\boldsymbol{e})\ \text{by symmetry}}+a(\boldsymbol{w}^h,\boldsymbol{w}^h).
$$

4. **Kill the cross term with part (a):** $a(\boldsymbol{w}^h,\boldsymbol{e})=0$ because $\boldsymbol{w}^h\in\mathcal{V}^h$. So

$$
a(\boldsymbol{U}^h-\boldsymbol{u},\,\boldsymbol{U}^h-\boldsymbol{u})=a(\boldsymbol{e},\boldsymbol{e})+a(\boldsymbol{w}^h,\boldsymbol{w}^h)\;\ge\;a(\boldsymbol{e},\boldsymbol{e}),
$$

   since $a(\boldsymbol{w}^h,\boldsymbol{w}^h)\ge0$. $\blacksquare$

**Two things Hughes's proof leaves between the lines:**

- **It is strict.** Equality needs $a(\boldsymbol{w}^h,\boldsymbol{w}^h)=0$. By (iii) (norm equivalence, positivity) that forces $\boldsymbol{w}^h=\boldsymbol{0}$, i.e. $\boldsymbol{U}^h=\boldsymbol{u}^h$. So $\boldsymbol{u}^h$ is the **unique** best, not merely "among the best." In our bar, $a(w^h,w^h)=K(d-\tfrac18)^2$: the "extra climb" in the widget.
- **Where each assumption was used.** (i): step 1 (that $\boldsymbol{w}^h$ is a test function) and part (a) (using $\boldsymbol{w}^h$ in the exact equation). (ii): bilinearity in (a); symmetry in step 3. (iii): uniqueness above.

Here is the picture that you now know how to read. It's the Part 1 projection picture, with Hughes's names on it:

  <text x="300" y="30" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" opacity=".8">a(Uʰ−u, Uʰ−u) = a(e, e) + a(wʰ, wʰ) ≥ a(e, e)</text>
